newsitem.title: USA: Ethics panel denies decision made in Gingrich case.
newsitem.headline: Ethics panel denies decision made in Gingrich case.

text.p: The special counsel for an ethics committee panel denied news reports on Thursday that it had agreed on what punishment to recommend for House Speaker Newt Gingrich for ethics violations.

"There have been recent press reports concerning the work of the Investigative Subcommittee and any recommendation it might make," James Cole said in a written statement. "Those statements and reports are not accurate."

News reports earlier said the four members of an ethics subcommittee -- two Republicans and two Democrats -- had agreed they would recommend to the full committee that it seek a reprimand of Gingrich.

Under committee rules a reprimand is appropriate for "serious violations" of House ethics rules but is less severe that the penalties of expulsion or censure. It would not require that Gingrich step down as speaker.
Cole said ethics rules did not permit public comment on the committee's work until it was convened in open session.
"All judgments should be withheld pending review of this matter in the course of the open sanction hearing," he said.

House Democratic Whip David Bonior also denied a decision had been made and accused Republicans of leaking the report in "one more desperate attempt ... to shore up the speaker's crumbling credibility in the light of his own admission that he lied to Congress and lied to the American people."

Following a two-year investigation the subcommittee said Dec. 21 that Gingrich had provided misleading information to investigators and had failed to ensure tax-exempt funds were not used for partisan purposes.
The full ethics committee must recommend a punishment to the full House but will not begin this process until after Gingrich seeks re-election as speaker when Congress convenes Tuesday.
Bonior, a leading Democratic critic of Gingrich, said the news report on Thursday "is inaccurate and untrue."
He said he had spoken to members of the ethics committee with an intimate knowledge of the Gingrich case and they had assured him that the news report was wrong.
"I expect members of the committee will soon clarify this mistake," he said.
